nodes.label: New Media
nodes.description: The convergence of computing and media technologies into numerical data.

nodes.label: Numerical Representation
nodes.description: All new media objects are composed of digital code and can be described formally.

nodes.label: Modularity
nodes.description: The 'fractal structure' of new media where elements maintain their separate identity.

nodes.label: Automation
nodes.description: A key principle of new media (listed).

nodes.label: Variability
nodes.description: A key principle of new media (listed).

nodes.label: Transcoding
nodes.description: A key principle of new media (listed).

nodes.label: Digitization
nodes.description: The process of converting continuous data into a numerical representation.

nodes.label: Sampling
nodes.description: Turning continuous data into discrete data.

nodes.label: Quantization
nodes.description: Assigning a numerical value to a sample.

nodes.label: Dziga Vertov
nodes.description: Avant-garde filmmaker, created Man with a Movie Camera.

nodes.label: Kino-Eye
nodes.description: Vertov's concept of using the camera to decode the world.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.description: A form or logic of new media; Vertov is cited as a 'database filmmaker'.

nodes.label: Low-level Automation
nodes.description: Automation where users modify or create media using templates or simple algorithms, standard in commercial software like Photoshop and Word.

nodes.label: High-level Automation
nodes.description: Automation requiring a computer to understand semantics, often using AI, as seen in game AI engines or virtual actors.

nodes.label: Scalability
nodes.description: A case of variability where versions of an object are generated at various sizes or levels of detail.

nodes.label: Hypermedia
nodes.description: A structure where media elements are connected via hyperlinks, separating elements from structure, seen as a case of variability.

nodes.label: Cultural Layer
nodes.description: The layer of media featuring recognizable objects, narratives, and traditional human meanings.

nodes.label: Computer Layer
nodes.description: The layer of media consisting of data structures, algorithms, variables, and machine-readable code.

nodes.label: Software Studies
nodes.description: A new stage in media theory turning to computer science to understand programmable media.

nodes.label: Cinema as Precursor
nodes.description: Cinema anticipated new media via discrete sampling of time, multimedia combinations, and random access mapping.

nodes.label: Myth of Lossless Copies
nodes.description: The notion that digital media copies identically, which is contradicted in reality by the pervasive use of lossy compression.

nodes.label: Lossy Compression
nodes.description: Techniques to reduce file size by deleting information, serving as the actual foundation of computer culture.

nodes.label: Interactivity Myth
nodes.description: The idea that 'interactive media' is unique to computers, ignoring that all HCI is interactive and older art forms required psychological interaction.

nodes.label: Externalization of Mind
nodes.description: The modern trend to objectify internal mental processes (like associations) into external visual forms or hyperlinked structures.

nodes.label: Human-Computer Interface (GUI)
nodes.description: A key semiotic code that filters all culture, imposing its own logic and blurring the work-leisure divide.

nodes.label: Cultural Interfaces
nodes.description: Human-computer-culture interfaces used for distributing and interacting with cultural data.

nodes.label: Human-Computer Interface (HCI)
nodes.description: General-purpose tool and metaphors (like the desktop) for operating a computer.

nodes.label: Printed Word
nodes.description: Tradition of text organization, pages, and hyperlinking providing a model for cultural interfaces.

nodes.label: Cinema
nodes.description: Tradition of mobile camera, framing, and narrative spatialization, increasingly dominating cultural interfaces.

nodes.label: Screen
nodes.description: A flat, rectangular surface positioned at a distance from the viewer, acting as a window into virtual spaces.

nodes.label: Classical Screen
nodes.description: Displays a static image separated from reality by a frame, like a painting.

nodes.label: Dynamic Screen
nodes.description: Displays a changing image of the past, capturing viewer's attention, like cinema.

nodes.label: Real-Time Screen
nodes.description: Displays an image updated in real time tracking a referent, like radar.

nodes.label: Interactive Screen
nodes.description: A screen where user actions can change computer memory and affect reality, like modern HCI.

nodes.label: Spatialization
nodes.description: The flattening of time into a navigable spatial landscape, common in new media.

nodes.label: Screen-based Apparatuses
nodes.description: Technologies like camera obscura, photography, and cinema that separate virtual and physical spaces and require viewer immobility. Belongs to Representation Tradition.

nodes.label: Virtual Reality (VR)
nodes.description: A screen-less apparatus that requires viewer movement while physically tethering them, blending or overriding physical space. Belongs to Simulation Tradition.

nodes.label: Simulation Tradition
nodes.description: A representational logic that blends virtual and physical spaces without a separating frame, allowing continuous scale (e.g., frescoes, VR).

nodes.label: Representation Tradition
nodes.description: A logic that separates physical and virtual spaces with a screen/frame, splitting the subject's identity (e.g., Renaissance painting, cinema).

nodes.label: New Media Operations
nodes.description: General techniques for working with computer media, such as selection, compositing, and teleaction, which become cognitive strategies.

nodes.label: Logic of Selection
nodes.description: A model of authorship based on choosing from pre-defined menus, libraries, and databases rather than authentic creation from scratch.

nodes.label: Electronic Signal Mutability
nodes.description: The inherent mutability of electronic signals that can be modified in real-time through filters, acting as a precursor to new media variability.

nodes.label: Digital Compositing
nodes.description: The operation of assembling disparate modular elements into a single seamless object, hiding their diverse origins.

nodes.label: Modular Media
nodes.description: Media formats (like 3D scenes, QuickTime) that maintain independent elements/layers, contrasting with traditional single-stream media.

nodes.label: Aesthetics of Continuity
nodes.description: An anti-montage aesthetics in new media where boundaries between elements are erased to simulate a continuous human experience.

nodes.label: Montage
nodes.description: A technique aiming to create visual, stylistic, semantic, and emotional dissonance by juxtaposing elements.

nodes.label: Montage within a shot (Spatial Montage)
nodes.description: Combining separate realities into contingent parts of a single image, making space as important as time.

nodes.label: Teleaction (Telepresence)
nodes.description: The ability to manipulate physical reality over a distance in real time through electronic transmission.

nodes.label: Image-Instruments
nodes.description: Representations (like perspective, radar, or real-time video) that systematically capture reality to act upon it.

nodes.label: Big Optics
nodes.description: Paul Virilio's concept of real-time electronic transmission that collapses physical distance.

nodes.label: Small Optics
nodes.description: Geometric perspective and human vision which maintain a natural spatial distance.

nodes.label: Synthetic Realism
nodes.description: The realistic representation of a different reality (cyborg/computer vision) rather than natural reality; conceptually pioneered by Georges Méliès.

nodes.label: Photorealism (Computer Graphics)
nodes.description: The ability of computer imagery to simulate the photographic lens (including its artifacts like depth of field, motion blur) rather than direct human perception.

nodes.label: Jurassic Park (Aesthetic)
nodes.description: The technique of artificially degrading perfect computer-generated graphics to match the grain and flaws of traditional film. Compared to Socialist Realism.

nodes.label: Socialist Realism
nodes.description: The superimposition of a perfect, idealized future onto the flawed, everyday present, analogous to Jurassic Park blending perfect CG with grainy film.

nodes.label: Meta-realism
nodes.description: A new realism based on the cyclical oscillation between an illusion and its suspension or destruction, typical of interactive media.

nodes.label: Phatic Function (Contact)
nodes.description: Communication dominated by the physical channel and act of connection, evident in web delays and loading sequences where the machine reveals itself.

nodes.label: Cognitive Multitasking
nodes.description: The rapid alternation between different kinds of attention and mental sets demanded by modern human-computer interfaces and interactive media.

nodes.label: Cinematic Realism
nodes.description: A historical standard of illusionism striving for a total approximation of reality (Bazin) or a substitution of codes (Comolli) driven by industrial aims (Bordwell & Staiger).

nodes.label: Image-Interface / Image-Instrument
nodes.description: Images transformed from passive representations into active tools that the user interacts with or uses to control reality.

nodes.label: Narrative
nodes.description: A cause-and-effect trajectory of events that creates a unique trajectory through a database, often de-materialized in new media.

nodes.label: Algorithm
nodes.description: A final sequence of simple operations executed by a computer to accomplish a task. Drives interactive narratives and games.

nodes.label: Data Structure
nodes.description: Data organized in a particular way for efficient search and retrieval, complementary to algorithms.

nodes.label: Paradigm
nodes.description: A set of related elements from which choices are made (implicit in traditional media, explicitly materialized in new media databases).

nodes.label: Syntagm
nodes.description: A linear sequence or combination of signs, representing the actualized narrative trajectory.

nodes.label: Navigable Space
nodes.description: A 3D virtual environment where navigation through space becomes a central action for narrative and exploration.

nodes.label: Computer Space
nodes.description: Virtual 3D environments generated by computers, often characterized by separate objects rather than a continuous spatial medium.

nodes.label: Aggregate Space
nodes.description: A discontinuous space composed of discrete entities, objects, or levels, lacking a unified systematic perspective (akin to ancient Greek space). Typical of the Web and virtual worlds.

nodes.label: Systematic Space
nodes.description: Infinite, homogeneous, continuous space that exists prior to objects, associated with Renaissance perspective.

nodes.label: Space-Medium
nodes.description: The concept of an environment where objects and space are embedded into an inseparable dense field (prostranstvennaya sreda), lacking distinct rigid boundaries.

nodes.label: The Flâneur
nodes.description: The modern urban observer who finds home in the anonymous crowd, navigating city spaces; reincarnated in new media as the Net surfer or Data Dandy.

nodes.label: The Explorer
nodes.description: The lonely hero navigating wilderness or unknown territories to build character and map space; reincarnated in new media as the player of computer games.

nodes.label: Flight Simulator
nodes.description: A military training technology that historically pioneered the interactive navigation of simulated spatial environments.

nodes.label: Non-place
nodes.description: Spaces of transit, contractuality, and impermanence (e.g., airports, highways, Web navigation) produced by supermodernity, animated by trajectories of moving bodies.

nodes.label: Supermodernity
nodes.description: A contemporary condition characterized by trajectories, flows, databases, and non-places, superseding modern forms of narrative and stable architecture.

nodes.label: Digital Cinema
nodes.description: Cinema created using digital technologies like 3D animation, digital compositing, and painting, changing its identity from indexical recording to a subset of animation.

nodes.label: Computer-based Image
nodes.description: An image that is discrete, modular, mathematically defined, and functions as both a representation and an interactive interface.

nodes.label: Traditional Cinema
nodes.description: The art of the index based on photographic recording, sequence narrative, and temporal montage.

nodes.label: Animation
nodes.description: A form relying on constructed, modified, or hand-painted images, discontinuous space, and discrete motion, which now forms the basis of digital cinema.

nodes.label: Loop
nodes.description: A repetitive temporal structure used in early moving pictures, computer programming, and new media narrative as an engine for interactive story progression.

nodes.label: Spatial Montage
nodes.description: A mode of juxtaposition where multiple images co-exist simultaneously on a screen, mirroring GUI logic and challenging linear cinematic narrative.

nodes.label: Cinegratography
nodes.description: A hybrid language merging cinematic illusionism and graphic collage aesthetics, heavily explored in CD-ROM interactive media.

nodes.label: Database Narrative
nodes.description: A narrative formed by accessing and streaming records from a database in real time.

nodes.label: Cinema as Information Space
nodes.description: The interpretation of cinema as an interface to events taking place in 3D space, similar to how new media interfaces present dense information.

nodes.label: Aesthetics of Density
nodes.description: A visual style characterized by a high density of information or objects, evident in web portals, GUI interfaces, and multi-layered digital films.

nodes.label: Dutch Painting (17th Century)
nodes.description: A historical precursor to the aesthetics of density, focused on detailed description and cataloging objects rather than hierarchical narration.

nodes.label: Christian Boustani's Films
nodes.description: Computer films that develop the aesthetics of density through digital compositing, using hundreds of layers to achieve unprecedented information density in cinema.

nodes.label: Cinema as a Code
nodes.description: The realization that in the computer age, cinema and other cultural forms become digital code (data) used to communicate experiences.

nodes.label: ASCII Films (Vuk Cosic)
nodes.description: Artworks that perform the new status of media as digital data by visibly displaying the ASCII code alongside the film image.

nodes.label: Media Translation
nodes.description: The continuous process of translating media content between formats, often resurrected as obsolete media in net.art.

nodes.label: Cultural Open Source
nodes.description: The effect of computerization that opens up traditional cultural techniques for redefinition, such as database challenging narrative and spatial montage challenging temporal montage.
